items.dose_gap: A 1,000 IU (25 µg) daily capsule needs about 150 g of cooked sockeye salmon or 155 g of grilled herring every single day. A 4,000 IU (100 µg) capsule needs roughly 600 g of sockeye salmon, 620 g of grilled herring, 46 large egg yolks, or about 1 kg of UV-treated portabella mushrooms daily. A 50,000 IU (1,250 µg) weekly loading dose, standard for correcting deficiency, has no food equivalent at all: it is about 7.8 kg of grilled herring. Real intakes are nowhere near this. UK NDNS figures cited by SACN put mean vitamin D intake from food at 2.8 µg/day in adults aged 19 to 65 and 3.3 µg/day in over-65s, which is 28% and 33% of the 10 µg RNI, and mean intakes have stayed below the RNI in every age group. Above roughly 50 degrees north, cutaneous synthesis is effectively zero from October to March, so there is no sunlight to make up the shortfall in winter. SACN's own conclusion was that the 10 µg RNI is difficult to achieve from natural food sources, which is why year-round or autumn/winter supplementation is advised for the whole UK population. Anyone with a diagnosed deficiency will not eat their way out of it at a northern latitude.
items.form_caveat: Mushroom vitamin D is D2 (ergocalciferol), a different molecule from the D3 in fish, egg yolk and almost all supplements, and D3 raises serum 25(OH)D more effectively than D2, with the gap widest for intermittent bolus dosing (Tripkovic et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012;95:1357-64, PMID 22552031, DOI 10.3945/ajcn.111.031070). UV mushroom content is also wildly variable and usually unlabelled: USDA measured UV-treated portabella at 3.4 µg/100 g from one producer and 25.6 µg/100 g from another, and maitake from 0.1 to 56.1 µg/100 g depending on the growing method, while untreated white mushrooms sit at 0.1 µg/100 g. Buying ordinary mushrooms because 'mushrooms have vitamin D' gets you essentially nothing. Cod liver oil is nominally a food but behaves as a supplement and carries 18,000 µg retinol per 100 g (CoFID 17-488), so a tablespoon delivers about 8,160 IU of preformed vitamin A alongside the D3, which rules it out in pregnancy. Oily fish delivers D3 inside a fat matrix with EPA/DHA, protein, iodine and selenium; a capsule delivers D3 alone.
items.bioavailability: Vitamin D from both food and capsules is fat-soluble and absorbed better with a meal containing fat, which oily fish and egg yolk supply themselves. The form matters more than the source: D2 from mushrooms is less effective per microgram than D3 (PMID 22552031). Egg yolk additionally contains 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (0.36 µg/100 g, CoFID 12-939), an already-hydroxylated metabolite that supplements normally do not provide. Total vitamin D figures in composition tables often bundle 25-OH-D3 with cholecalciferol, so a headline 'vitamin D' number for eggs or canned salmon is not strictly comparable to the D3 in a capsule.

items.dose_gap: 400 IU of natural vitamin E is 268 mg of RRR-alpha-tocopherol. Reaching that from food, every day, means about 720 g of sunflower seeds (roughly 4,200 kcal), or 1.05 kg of almonds, or 201 g of wheatgerm oil (about 15 tablespoons of neat oil), or 550 g of sunflower oil. If the capsule is synthetic all-rac (180 mg for 400 IU), it is still 484 g of sunflower seeds or 10 tablespoons of wheatgerm oil daily. No dietary pattern gets there: habitual intakes cluster around 5 to 20 mg/day, so 400 IU sits one to two orders of magnitude above anything eating produces. This is a pharmacological dose with no dietary analogue, and it cannot be reached by eating.
items.form_caveat: Most 400 IU capsules contain all-rac-alpha-tocopheryl acetate, a synthetic mixture of eight stereoisomers of which only one eighth is the RRR form that human alpha-tocopherol transfer protein preferentially retains. Food contains only RRR. That difference is precisely why the label conversions differ (1 IU = 0.67 mg natural versus 0.45 mg synthetic). Food also never delivers alpha-tocopherol in isolation: sunflower oil carries 48.7 mg alpha with 5.1 mg gamma per 100 g, while rapeseed oil carries 18.4 mg alpha with 38.0 mg gamma (CoFID 17-045, 17-041), and nuts add tocotrienols. High-dose alpha-tocopherol actively removes part of what food supplies: 400 IU/day of RRR-alpha-tocopheryl acetate cut serum gamma-tocopherol by a median 58% and reduced detectable delta-tocopherol in a randomised placebo-controlled trial of 184 adults (Huang et al., J Nutr 2003;133:3137-40, PMID 14519797). A 400 IU capsule is therefore not a concentrated version of a handful of sunflower seeds; it changes the balance of vitamin E forms in blood in a direction food never does.
items.bioavailability: Alpha-tocopherol needs dietary fat and bile for absorption, which nuts and oils supply intrinsically, so food forms are absorbed efficiently in ordinary meals. Fractional absorption falls as the single dose rises, and hepatic alpha-TTP selectively retains only the 2R stereoisomers, so the 2S half of a synthetic all-rac dose is largely excreted. The practical consequence is that the useful fraction of a 400 IU synthetic capsule is well below its stated IU, and the plasma alpha-tocopherol achieved does not scale linearly with dose, while the displacement of gamma- and delta-tocopherol documented by Huang et al. (PMID 14519797) does.

items.availability_note: Liver is far more concentrated in preformed retinol than the supplement: 10,000 IU is 3,000 µg retinol, and every common liver measured in the UK tables contains 10,500 to 25,200 µg per 100 g. This is the one item in this set where the food beats the pill, which is exactly why liver carries a public-health warning rather than a recommendation.

items.dose_gap: There is no gap to close. Twelve grams of fried calf liver supplies the full 3,000 µg (10,000 IU) of a high-dose retinol capsule, and a normal 100 g portion of any liver delivers 3.5 to 8.4 times that dose in a single sitting. A 40 g serving of liver pate is functionally a 10,000 IU tablet. A tablespoon of cod liver oil is 8,160 IU. Anyone eating liver weekly is already taking supraphysiological preformed vitamin A intermittently, and adding a 10,000 IU supplement on top compounds a load the body stores rather than clears. For context, the US tolerable upper intake level for preformed vitamin A is 3,000 µg/day, which is the supplement dose itself, and the UK RNI is 700 µg for men and 600 µg for women.
items.form_caveat: The retinol in liver is the same molecule as the retinyl palmitate or acetate in capsules, absorbed by the same route and stored in the liver in the same way, so the usual reassurance that 'food forms are safer' does not apply here. Pregnancy is the sharp edge: UK advice is that people who are pregnant or who might become pregnant should avoid liver and liver products including pate, and should avoid supplements containing vitamin A including fish liver oils, because excess retinol is teratogenic (NHS pregnancy vitamins guidance; UK Committee on Toxicity statement on vitamin A in the maternal diet, TOX-2021-57). Cod liver oil is the common trap because it is bought for omega-3 or vitamin D and delivers 60,000 IU of retinol per 100 g. Outside pregnancy, chronic preformed retinol above the 3,000 µg/day UL is associated with reduced bone mineral density and fracture risk, which is why UK advice is to eat liver no more than once a week rather than to eat more of it. Beta-carotene-rich foods are the safe substitute precisely because their conversion is regulated (see the beta-carotene entry).
items.bioavailability: Retinyl esters from liver and from supplements are absorbed at high efficiency and, critically, absorption is not down-regulated when stores are full, so intake accumulates in hepatic stellate cells over weeks and months. This is the opposite of carotenoid absorption, which is feedback-limited through retinoic-acid induction of the intestinal transcription factor ISX and consequent repression of SR-B1 and BCO1 (reviewed in Nutrients 2019;11(4):838, DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). Cooking concentrates liver retinol rather than destroying it: CoFID shows raw lamb liver at 17,300 µg/100 g rising to 19,700 µg/100 g fried, and raw ox liver at 14,200 rising to 17,300 stewed, through water loss (codes 18-413, 18-494, 18-415, 18-416).

items.dose_gap: By raw mass the trial doses are reachable: 20 mg/day is about 219 g of raw carrot (roughly three and a half medium carrots) or 360 g of boiled sweet potato, and 30 mg/day is about 312 g of carrot. By absorbed dose it is a different story. The Dietary Reference Intake conversion factors treat 12 µg of food beta-carotene as equivalent to 1 µg retinol activity, against 2 µg for supplemental beta-carotene in oil, implying the supplement form is about six times more available (Institute of Medicine, DRIs for Vitamin A and related micronutrients, 2001, DOI 10.17226/10026). Matching the absorbed exposure of a 20 mg capsule therefore takes on the order of 120 mg of food beta-carotene, roughly 1.3 kg of raw carrots every day, which nobody eats and which the gut would not absorb anyway. So the honest answer is that food matches the label number and does not match the plasma exposure that produced the trial results.
items.form_caveat: This is the clearest food-versus-extract case in the set. Supplement beta-carotene is synthetic all-trans-beta-carotene or algal/fungal beta-carotene, formulated in oil or water-dispersible beadlets specifically to defeat the poor bioavailability of the food form, so it is engineered to do what a carrot cannot. Food never delivers beta-carotene alone: the same carrot supplies 5,230 µg/100 g of alpha-carotene (CoFID 13-496), and dark greens supply lutein with far less beta-carotene. Dietary carotenoids carry none of the supplement harm for three reasons. First, uptake and cleavage are feedback-regulated: absorbed beta-carotene raises intracellular retinoic acid, which induces ISX, which represses SR-B1 and BCO1 in the enterocyte, so absorption falls as vitamin A status rises (Nutrients 2019;11(4):838, DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). A capsule of purified beta-carotene in oil pushes plasma concentrations well past anything food produces. Second, the harm signals came from isolated high doses in high-risk groups: 20 mg/day raised lung cancer incidence by 18% in male smokers (ATBC, N Engl J Med 1994;330:1029-35, PMID 8127329, DOI 10.1056/nejm199404143301501) and 30 mg/day plus 25,000 IU retinyl palmitate produced 28% more lung cancers, RR 1.36, in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers (CARET, J Natl Cancer Inst 1996;88:1550, PMID 8901853, DOI 10.1093/jnci/88.21.1550). CARET cannot even be attributed to beta-carotene alone, since it co-administered a large preformed retinol dose. Third, overloading on carrots produces carotenodermia, a harmless orange discolouration of the skin, rather than hypervitaminosis A, because the conversion step is regulated. 'Eat carrots' and 'take 20 mg of beta-carotene' are not the same intervention.
items.bioavailability: Beta-carotene in raw carrot and raw spinach is locked in chromoplasts behind intact plant cell walls, so absorption from raw vegetables is low; chopping, pureeing, cooking and eating with fat all raise it, and cooking does not destroy it (CoFID shows boiled old carrot at 9,616 µg/100 g against 9,149 raw, codes 13-497 and 13-496, reflecting water loss and retention). The formal expression of this is the 12:1 food versus 2:1 supplement-in-oil conversion factor (IOM 2001, DOI 10.17226/10026). Conversion efficiency also varies substantially between individuals through BCO1 genotype and vitamin A status, which is why plasma responses to the same carrot intake differ several-fold between people (DOI 10.3390/nu11040838). Spinach deserves a specific caution: it is the textbook carotenoid green, but baby spinach carries only 1,559 µg/100 g raw, well under a fifth of carrot, and its oxalate load makes it a poor recommendation for people managing kidney stones.

items.dose_gap: The two forms give opposite answers, which is why they must not be merged. MK-7 at the doses used in supplements and trials, 90 to 180 µg/day, is fully covered by food: one 50 g pack of natto is 470 µg of MK-7, so a pack every second or third day matches a 180 µg capsule. Nothing else does. Matching 180 µg/day from cheddar at 2.7 µg/100 g would take 6.7 kg of cheese a day, and from butter about 4.3 kg. MK-4 is the reverse. The clinical dose in Japan, menatetrenone for osteoporosis, is 45 mg/day (45,000 µg), typically 15 mg three times daily. At the richest measured food value, barbecue chicken at 22.1 µg/100 g, that is about 204 kg of chicken per day. Even a modest 1.5 mg consumer MK-4 pill needs 6.8 kg of chicken or 58 kg of whole milk. Measured whole-diet MK-4 intake sits around 17 µg/day (7.3% of a mean total vitamin K intake of about 230 µg/day in Japanese women, Kamao 2007), which is roughly one 2,600th of the pharmacological dose. MK-4 at supplement strength is unreachable by eating, and no amount of butter, egg yolk or chicken changes that.
items.form_caveat: MK-7 supplements are made by Bacillus subtilis natto fermentation, the same organism that makes natto, or synthesised; the active species is all-trans MK-7 and cis-isomer contamination is a documented quality problem in commercial products that the fermented food does not have. MK-4 supplements are wholly synthetic, derived from menadione, because no food is or could be concentrated to 45 mg per dose. Natto also brings the fermentation matrix, fibre and nattokinase, and circulating K2 after eating natto is around ten times the circulating K1 after eating spinach (Schurgers LJ, Vermeer C, Haemostasis 2000;30:298-307, PMID 11356998). The common 'cheese is a K2 food' claim needs unpicking: cheese total vitamin K is genuinely high, 282 µg/100 g for hard cheese and up to 506 µg/100 g for soft cheese, but roughly 90% of it is MK-9, MK-10 and MK-11 from starter bacteria (Fu et al. 2017, PMID 29955705), forms that no clinical trial has tested, while the MK-7 fraction is only a few µg/100 g. Animal MK-4 also tracks the animal's feed: menadione is a routine poultry feed additive and Elder et al. attribute poultry MK-4 to alkylation of that menadione, so brand, country and production system shift the numbers, and the two chicken hot dog and chicken broth samples in the same study contained no detectable MK-4 at all.
items.bioavailability: MK-4 and MK-7 behave so differently that microgram-for-microgram comparison is meaningless. A single 420 µg dose of MK-7 was well absorbed and remained detectable in serum for 48 hours, whereas the identical 420 µg dose of MK-4 was undetectable in serum, and over seven days of 60 µg/day only MK-7 raised serum concentrations (Sato T et al., Nutr J 2012;11:93, PMID 23140417, DOI 10.1186/1475-2891-11-93). MK-7's long half-life comes from its extended isoprenoid side chain and tight lipoprotein binding. This is the mechanistic reason MK-4 must be dosed in milligrams while MK-7 works in micrograms, and it means the 1 to 22 µg/100 g of MK-4 in butter, egg yolk, cheese and chicken contributes almost nothing to circulating vitamin K2 even though it is real and measurable. All menaquinones need dietary fat for absorption, which is why they are found in and absorbed from the fat phase of dairy and eggs; the reduced-fat versions lose most of it, with reduced-fat cheddar at 1.8 µg MK-4 per 100 g against 9.5 µg for full fat (PMID 29955705).

misclassifications: Vitamin E at or above 400 IU/d classified RICH: wrong for the item as scoped. The classification describes the nutrient, but the item is defined by its dose, and the entry's own dose_gap says 'This is a pharmacological dose with no dietary analogue, and it cannot be reached by eating.' A label of RICH sitting above that sentence is self-contradictory. Alpha-tocopherol at RDA level is genuinely rich in food; 400 IU is not obtainable from any diet. This needs a dose-aware class (nutrient rich in food, supplement dose unreachable), not RICH.

Vitamin K2 '(MK-7 and MK-4)' classified RICH as one merged item: two forms with opposite answers cannot share one availability class. MK-7 at 90 to 180 µg is genuinely food-reachable, but only from natto, so the RICH label rests on exactly one food that most of the target population never eats; every other MK-7 source listed is trace (cheddar 2.7, butter 4.2 µg/100 g). MK-4 at the 45 mg clinical dose is unreachable by a factor of thousands and the entry itself concedes 'MK-4 supplements are wholly synthetic, derived from menadione, because no food is or could be concentrated to 45 mg per dose.' Split into MK-7 = RICH (single-food dependency flagged) and MK-4 = synthetic/unreachable at clinical dose, trace in food.

Vitamin D3 classified RICH: defensible but borderline, and the entry does not acknowledge the tension. Two of the twelve 'foods' are not natural food sources at all: cod liver oil is conceded in the same entry to 'behave as a supplement', and fortified orange juice is a manufactured delivery vehicle. Strip those and one trace entry (untreated white mushrooms at 0.1 µg/100 g, under 1% of RNI), and the genuine dietary base narrows to oily fish plus egg yolk plus UV-treated mushrooms. Against that, the entry's own evidence is that population intake is 28 to 33% of the RNI and SACN concluded the RNI is 'difficult to achieve from natural food sources'. RICH is not wrong, but it should be qualified as 'rich in a narrow set of foods, and demonstrably not delivering the RNI at population level'.

Vitamin D3 food list omits the farmed-versus-wild distinction, which functions as a misclassification in practice: the entry anchors on wild sockeye at 16.7 µg/100 g, but farmed Atlantic salmon (what most shoppers actually buy) runs several-fold lower. Presenting sockeye as 'salmon' overstates what the typical purchase delivers.

Preformed vitamin A at or above 10,000 IU classified RICH: correct, and correctly reasoned. Liver genuinely exceeds the supplement dose and the entry draws the right conclusion (public-health warning, not recommendation). No change.

verification_report.net_assessment:
Process caveat first: the session's WebSearch quota was already fully consumed (200/200) before this task began, so the requested 8-plus searches were impossible. I substituted roughly 24 targeted WebFetch calls against PubMed, gov.uk and USDA FoodData Central mirrors. FDC's own site returned 404 on every food-detail route and the API rate-limited DEMO_KEY, so USDA values were read through an FDC mirror rather than the primary source, and no FDC ID could be resolved.

Strongest part of the submission by a wide margin is the literature. Every one of the ten checkable citations survived: Huang 2003 (400 IU, 184 nonsmokers, median 58% gamma-tocopherol fall), Kamao 2007 (natto 939 µg/100 g, 230 µg/d total K, MK-4 7.3%), Fu 2017 (hard cheese 282, soft 506 µg/100 g, MK-9/10/11 dominance), Sato 2012 (420 µg MK-4 undetectable), Tripkovic 2012 (D3 over D2, bolus-specific), Schurgers 2000, Roberts 2008, ATBC/CARET, and the Nutrients 2019 DOI, which resolves to a genuine Reboul review. The CARET figure is the notable case: I expected RR 1.36 to be an error against the commonly quoted 1.28, and the cited JNCI paper genuinely reports 1.36 for weighted incidence. Whoever wrote this read the papers.

Arithmetic is also strong. Of roughly 90 recomputable figures, only two are actually wrong: 30 mg beta-carotene from raw carrot is 328 g not 312 g (raw/boiled values silently swapped mid-sentence), and 1.5 mg MK-4 from whole milk is 150 kg not 58 kg, an error by a factor of 2.6 that understates the entry's own case. One rounding is loose (890 g of UV portabella, stated as 1 kg). The CoFID total-vitamin-D convention (cholecalciferol + 5 x 25-OH-D3) and the alpha-tocopherol-equivalents convention both make several figures look like addition errors when they are not, and the submission applies both correctly.

The real weakness is the food-composition layer, and it is systematic rather than random. CoFID carries most of the numeric load and not one of its 35 food codes could be confirmed. Where USDA was reachable, six foods diverged by 2x to 4x, and five of the six run in the direction that flatters the entry's narrative: egg yolk vitamin D overstated 2.4x, butter beta-carotene overstated 3.9x, butter retinol 43% high, while olive oil vitamin E is understated 2.8x, baked sweet potato beta-carotene 2.24x and dried apricots 3.4x. Raw spinach is understated 3.6x, which falsifies an explicit comparative claim ('well under a fifth of carrot' is really about two-thirds against USDA). Herring vitamin D, an anchor for two dose-gap calculations, is 3x above USDA's Atlantic herring. Two citations could not be found at all: COT TOX-2021-57 and the NDNS 2.8/3.3 µg intake figures.

Two classification calls need changing. Vitamin E at 400 IU is labelled RICH directly above a dose_gap that says it 'cannot be reached by eating', which is self-contradictory for a dose-defined item. And merging MK-7 and MK-4 under one RICH label buries the fact that MK-4 at 45 mg is synthetic-only by the entry's own admission, while MK-7's RICH status depends entirely on natto. Vitamin D3's RICH is defensible but should be qualified, since three of its twelve entries are a supplement, a fortified vehicle and a trace food.

One factual error carries real weight: barbecue chicken is not the richest MK-4 food. Goose liver paste at roughly 369 µg/100 g is about 17x higher and also defeats the claim that 'no food comes within three orders of magnitude' of the 45 mg dose (it is about 2.1 orders). The conclusion still holds at 12.2 kg/day, so the argument survives, but the supporting statement is wrong and the food is missing from the list. Alongside it, the omission of UV maitake at 56.1 µg/100 g is odd because the entry cites that number in its own caveat, and the UK-framed vitamin D and vitamin A entries both omit fortified fat spreads, which is where a large share of UK intake actually comes from.

Verdict: the reasoning, the pharmacology and the citation discipline are well above average, and the qualitative conclusions are all sound and would survive every correction above. The numbers are not yet trustworthy at the precision they are quoted to. Before publication I would require a direct read of the CoFID spreadsheet to confirm the 35 codes, replacement of the six USDA-divergent values with sourced ranges, the two arithmetic fixes, the two classification splits, correction of the richest-MK-4-food claim, and removal or replacement of the TOX-2021-57 and NDNS references. Confidence in my own USDA comparisons is moderate rather than high, since they came through a mirror; the citation verifications are high confidence.
